Background:
When choosing the design for our hull, we used a decision matrix to weigh the options
seeing how almost everyone was new to boats and/or RC racing. We picked out the categories
we felt were most important to the competition and did research on all the possible boat options.

Figure 1 – Decision Matrix

Once the Inboard Catamaran was chosen, we started researching how to make a racing
catamaran optimized for the challenge given to us. The challenge being traveling 2 miles in
semi-open water with 3 turns all while carrying a 60-pound payload. We felt as though
prioritizing stability and efficiency would give us the best chance as first year competitors. We
designed a deep pontoon on either side as our way of housing electrical components and the
payload, as well as a flatter yet enclosed bridge deck area that would house the ESC and rudder.
Tapering the front of the boat higher up would generate more lift and get the catamaran
on a higher riding plane. Paired the dual sponson design where less water comes in contact with
the boat, we are able to reduce lots of hydrodynamic drag.
We also wanted to take advantage of the strength that the dual sponson design has
because we will be dealing with wakes and possibly small waves depending on weather. This
design also allows forces and stress to be equally distributed across the boat without flipping or
rolling.
By analyzing the challenges and requirements for the race and using a decision matrix we
were able to choose the hull design and general layout of the components that we would later
build off with 3D rendering.

Design and Analysis:

pages.text:
4
The catamaran design was developed using Rhino CAD, with roughly eight design
iterations leading to the final configuration. The final design measures 6 feet in length, 2.5 feet in
width, and 1.5 feet in height. It features an inverted bow and dual chines on the outer edges of
each hull 6 (see Figures 1 through 3). The inverted bow was selected for its ability to reduce
resistance, enhance wave-piercing capability and increase the hull’s waterline length. All these
factors contribute to better hydrodynamic performance. Our goal was to create a watercraft
capable of planning efficiently, minimizing drag and maximizing speed. To assist with this, the
outer chines were added to provide flat surfaces that aid in pushing the craft onto plane. We used
Orca3D CFD software to simulate the vessel's buoyancy and planning performance. These
simulations were supported by feedback from a professional naval architect at Orca3D, who
helped validate our assumptions and refine our model (see Figures 4 through 6). The CFD results
indicated that with a total load of 150 pounds and at a target speed of 30 knots, the craft would
require approximately 6,000 Watts of effective power delivered to the water. This data was
instrumental in selecting appropriate motor and battery components capable of meeting
performance goals.

Figure 2 – Rhino CAD Model – Front View

Figure 3 – Rhino CAD Model – Side View

Build and Fabrication Process:
Inner components:
Keeping our Liperior 5000 mAH 12s 44.4v batteries and inner components low in each
of the pontoons keeps all our electrical except for the servo and transmitter in an accessible line
that can be sealed in a waterproof box to prevent any electrical hazards. Battery’s will be
strapped onto plates that are epoxied into the inside of the hull, this way removing and charging
is easy and efficient.

Figure 7 – 5000mAh 44.4V 12s Lipo Batterys

The powertrain in each pontoon rests at the bottom and starts with a 24s battery set up on
each side. This was done by having two 12s 44.4v Lipo Batteries run in parallel. Those are then
connected to TP 5680 850 KV brushless motors. These motors directly spin a flex cable that
comes through a coupler fastened to the stern of each pontoon that rotates the propeller at the end
of the boat.

Figure 8 – TP 850 KV Motor

Because this system draws immense amounts of heat, we are using two water pickups
with each pontoon, one jacket specifically for the ESC and one for the motor. By not reusing the
already warm water from jacket to the next it gives our electrical system cooler water to run
with, giving optimal motor output. Cooling will be tested and perfected by monitoring the
temperatures on increasingly longer runs.
For controlling the boat, we decided to use a BOCO RC Berserker 74kg 25T steel gear
servo. This servo is a very heavy-duty choice that is able to turn our 105mm rutter no matter the
drag forces acting on the boat. The servo is also directly compatible to our Hobbywing SeaKing
300A HV V4 Brushless Marine ESC, which can handle up to 14s so it would have no problem
with our 12s electrical system. Lastly for the remote we chose DX3 Smart 3-Channel Transmitter
paired with its SR315 Receiver

Figure 9 – 74kg Servo and 105 mm Rutter

Figure 10 – 300A Hobbywing ESC

We decided to use an aluminum 70mm 3 bladed CNC cut prop because it would provide
a good amount of thrust without overheating our motors. Aluminum was chosen because of how
light it is, as this makes for much more efficient propulsion.

Fabrication:
The design and fabrication of our fully electric, unmanned boat was a project that
required combining of computer-aided design (CAD), material science, fabrication techniques,
and performance-based decision making. Our objective was to create a fully electric, unmanned
catamaran boat that maximizes stability, minimizes drag, and maintains structural integrity,
while complying with all the rules and safety regulations required for the competition.
To create our boat, a CAD model was created using Rhino CAD, SolidWorks, and Orca
3D. Rhino CAD and SolidWorks allowed us to define the geometry of the hull, analyze
proportions, and create cross-sectional slices that were then used for fabrication. Orca 3D was
used to determine drag, buoyancy, and speed. The catamaran shape was selected due to its
improved stability and reduced drag force. The use of two very slim hulls over one very wide
hull significantly decreases the drag on the surface of the boat, allowing it to easily cut through
the water. Additionally, the wide base of a catamaran style boat provides a significant amount of
stability in comparison other designs.
From a hydrodynamic perspective, minimizing drag was one of our teams' primary
concerns. Our design utilizes a slender hull with smooth geometry. This will reduce turbulent
flow and maintain a more laminar flow across the hull. The combination between Orca 3D and
SolidWorks and Rhino CAD models helped ensure gradual curvature which is essential in
preventing turbulent flow and drag.
After finalizing the design, we moved into fabrication. Initially the team used a largescale 3D printer to create 5 separate pieces made of PETG filament. Due to the complex shape of
our hull, the 3D printer had a hard time forming many of the curves along the bow. With each
piece only being about 0.25 inches thick, there were many deformation issues. When initially
using small scale models to test the design, these problems did not occur. During the 3D printing
of the actual design there was also a slight warping from heat. Because of the fast-approaching
deadline, we decided to shift towards a different material, as the 3D print was not feasible for
this design.
The team decided to use Extruded polystyrene (XPS) foam as the core hull material. XPS
foam was selected due to its lightweight properties, ease of shaping, and resistance to water
absorption. This material is extremely buoyant and ensures that there is enough trapped air in the
boat such that if the entire boat is filled with water, it will still float. Using the cross-sectional
slices from the SolidWorks model, we cut the foam into precise sections with a hot knife, and
any excess material was removed with a hand saw and sanding blocks. The hot knife allowed us

pages.text:
8
to make controled cuts without tearing or compressing the material. This is critical for
maintaining dimensional accuracy.
After each two-inch slice was cut with the hot knife, we used a disk sander to perfect the
shape and create smooth transitions between each section. Symmetry is vital between the two
hulls for balanced hydrodynamic performance, as any slight difference can lead to uneven drag
forces, causing the boat to have difficulty steering and lose efficiency. Achieving perfect
symmetry became one of our greatest challenges as a team during the fabrication process. It
required continuous measurement, visual inspection, and sanding.
Once our foam sections were properly shaped, we glued them together using Loctite PL
300 Construction Foamboard Adhesive. This adhesive was specifically chosen because it is
chemically compatible with foam and provides a strong and flexible bond. The assembly process
required careful alignment of each section to maintain the shape of the original CAD model. Any
misalignment at this stage could compromise our boat’s performance and balance.
We applied multiple layers of fiberglass and epoxy to the hull with West System 105
epoxy resin and 206 slow hardener. This layering process significantly increased the strength and
durability of our boat. This outer fiberglass shell not only protects the foam core from water
intrusion, but also distributes the forces more evenly across the hull. Each layer was applied
carefully to avoid air bubbles and inconsistencies. These errors have the potential to weaken the
hull or create drag, so the surface finish is very important for the performance of our boat. A
smoother surface reduces drag, which is especially important at high speeds. Any roughness or
abnormality on the hull surface can create turbulent flow and increase resistance.
After the hull was fiber glassed, we incorporated PVC piping as internal reinforcement to
improve the structural integrity of the hull. The PVC is a lightweight structural frame, increasing
the rigidity of the boat. This helps it resist bending and torsional stresses. This reinforcement was
especially important due to the lack of rigidity of the XPS foam. The foam alone would not be
strong enough to withstand loads such as impact, propulsion forces, or handling stresses.
After the completion of our hull the team will conduct the first test. Our boat hull will be
placed in the water to ensure that the weight is distributed evenly. It is understood that even the
slightest inconsistency in the weight distribution of the boat can affect anything from speed to
steering capability. Although our buoyancy calculations came out successful in theory, this test
will confirm our calculations in practice. This test will prove that we had enough trapped air
within the XPS foam such that when the boat fills with water it does not sink. If the test is
unsuccessful and our boat is not buoyant, there are steps to ensure buoyancy. If the boat does
sink when we test it with the weight, then we can add more spray foam to ensure buoyancy. This
test will prove that we had enough trapped air within the XPS foam so that it does not sink.
Since the boat is fully electric and unmanned, additional considerations were given to
weight distribution and system integration. The placement of components such as the battery,

pages.text:
9
motor, and control systems needed to maintain a low center of gravity and proper balance
between the two hulls. An uneven weight distribution could negatively impact stability, increase
drag, or cause inefficient propulsion.
The propulsion system consists of dual TP 5870 750KV motors paired with stainless steel
shafts and controlled by a Seaking 300A ESC. This allows for a high number of rotations per
minute that will sufficiently propel the boat through the required course. Power is supplied by a
44.4V semi-solid-state lithium polymer battery. This was researched by the team and selected for
its high energy density and safety profile. The control system includes a Radiomaster MT12
transmitter and receiver, with a custom wire harness and emergency shutoff switch. This will be
placed towards the back of the boat in line with the two hulls, a few inches below the water line.
This will ensure the propellers will be below the waterline, and the shafts will experience less
stress.
Once the motor is installed, we will conduct our second test. This test will be used to
determine the true functionality of our motor as well as the speed of our boat. This test will be
conducted in our university recreational center pool. The boat will run 8 laps of the pool (200m)
to confirm its functionality.
Throughout this entire project, we strictly followed safety regulations to ensure the safety
of the members of our team. This included the safe handling of cutting tools such as the hot
knife, proper use of sanding equipment, and careful application of adhesives and epoxy
materials, which can produce harmful fumes if not used correctly. To reduce health risk from
fumes, respirator masks were worn by everyone in the room when fumes or excessive dust were
possible. Additionally, the final design complied with all competition guidelines for an
unmanned, fully electric vessel.

Risks:
The XPS foam used for the hull naturally contains ample trapped air as the material is
typically used for insulation. This trapped air makes the boat buoyant, such that if the boat were
to capsize, it would remain afloat. This mitigates potential risk for sinking or taking on water
while riding.
The catamaran hull we chose was designed with safety in mind. When comparing the risk
of rolling over between monohulls and catamarans, we saw that a dual sponson design would
mitigate that risk. In addition to a decreased chance of rolling over, the catamaran design is more
stable because of the balance between both sponsons. This reliability is necessary, especially
when carrying a 60-pound payload and heavy electrical components. Since the race is held at an
open water location, waves from wind and the wake of safety boats add additional forces to the
hull. A catamaran is more suitable for these rougher conditions than a typical speed boat or flat-

pages.text:
10
bottom boat design. The forces from the weights inside and those from waves led us to choose
the strength of the catamaran as a key point for risk mitigation.
Initially we chose to use 3D printed slices of our designed hull as the basis for our layers
of epoxy and fiber glass. After assessing the completed prints, we saw many errors in the 3d
printing process, such as a hollow space between the inner and outer wall of our hull. This was
meant to be solid. Additionally, the hull was printed extremely thin, which left space for
chipping, cracking, and disforming before we could reinforce the epoxy and fiberglass. These
structural issues caused an immediate risk to the integrity of our boat. We decided to use the
same catamaran design, but hand cut out foam slices using XPS insulation material. This way we
can control the thickness of the walls and rely on a hull that won’t morph over time before we
are able to fiberglass and epoxy it. Additionally, this allows the team to reap the benefits of more
buoyant material.
Prior to waterproofing the boat, we tested the XPS sheets and the Loctite PL300
foamboard glue in a bucket of water over a period of 24 hours to ensure water resistance and the
strength of the glue.
After ensuring the material and glue were compatible and durable, we waterproofed the
boat. The team chose to epoxy the outside of the hull, having glued all of the hand cut XPS slices
together. We tested epoxy and fiberglass on scrap XPS sheets, one on a flat surface, one on a
curved surface, and one on a flat surface with epoxy and a layer of fiberglass. This was done as a
precaution to ensure the most successful application method and to check if the epoxy was
compatible with the XPS material. Along with adding waterproof safety, this added much needed
structural integrity to the XPS base of the boat.

are able to fiberglass and epoxy it. Additionally, this allows the team to reap the benefits of more
buoyant material.
        Prior to waterproofing the boat, we tested the XPS sheets and the Loctite PL300
foamboard glue in a bucket of water over a period of 24 hours to ensure water resistance and the
strength of the glue.

        After ensuring the material and glue were compatible and durable, we waterproofed the
boat. The team chose to epoxy the outside of the hull, having glued all of the hand cut XPS slices
together. We tested epoxy and fiberglass on scrap XPS sheets, one on a flat surface, one on a
curved surface, and one on a flat surface with epoxy and a layer of fiberglass. This was done as a
precaution to ensure the most successful application method and to check if the epoxy was
compatible with the XPS material. Along with adding waterproof safety, this added much needed
structural integrity to the XPS base of the boat.

Figure 12- Epoxy and Fiberglass Testing

The race is in brackish water, which created new risks that needed to be addressed before
and after the race. Making sure the boat is clean and the components are lubricated prior to the
race is critical. All our testing has been in freshwater, meaning these procedures will be
performed very close to race day. Preceding the race, the boat will have to be cleaned, flushed
with freshwater (excluding the waterproof interior), and afterwards, left to completely dry.
According to our calculations, the buoyancy change due to differences in water type will be
negligible.
When addressing the risk of electrical shortages, we decided to add all waterproof boxes
to house all our electrical components. This will ensure that even if water were to get inside, or if
the boat capsized, then no components could shorten or start a fire.
Lastly, even though the Catamaran is a strong and reliable design, support inside would
still be important to prevent cracking along the center structure that connects the two 2 sponsons.
For this inner reinforcement, use PVC pipes running the length and width of the boat, somewhat
resembling Bulkheads and Stringers. This was to prevent any cracking from sheer or torsional
forces. These PVC pipes will be bonded to the inside of the boat with epoxy and fiberglass.

From these calculations we can see that the volume is enough to support the total weight,
including the 60-pound payload and the electronics, proving that the boat will successfully float.
With the added epoxy and fiberglass, the weight would still be within the calculated limit.
Therefore, buoyancy is not a primary concern. The main concern is the strength and
rigidity/durability of the boat. The material that we are using, XPS, is light but weak, so the
added epoxy helps strengthen the walls of the boat. However, with only XPS, glue, and epoxy,
the boat would not be strong enough to successfully compete in the competition. The added
fiberglass covering strengthens the hull for increased reliability. Overall, covering the XPS hull
with epoxy and a fiberglass shell will give us the most reliability and strength with additional
extra weight.
